records.title: Tom Friedman’s deceptive effort to lure Dems to escalate in Iran
records.summary: The centrist Democrats’ campaign to rescue - not end - Donald Trump’s illegal war with Iran has officially begun. Behold Tom Friedman’s column today in The New York Times. Tom puts forward an argument with a clever structure. He starts by blasting Trump’s decision to start the war. He cites numerous data points, including testimony from GCC officials that tears massive holes in the White House’s narrative that the situation is under control, that Iran is on the ropes, and that Trump has won the battle for the Strait of Hormuz. This paragraph, for instance: “I had a briefing from a senior Emirati oil official who shared with me a digital map of the relentless Iranian attacks on the fleet of Emirati-owned oil tankers — not when they pass through the Strait of Hormuz near Iran, but when they try to transit the Persian Gulf in Emirati waters, hugging the country’s eastern coastline. These are highly sophisticated attacks, mostly with cruise missiles and drones, that go right into the oil tankers’ engine rooms and disable them. Bull’s-eye every time. The Emirates then has to send tugboats out to rescue the crews and pull the disabled tankers into port. This is happening almost every day

records.title: The Guardian view on ‘two-tier policing’: tackle the myth, don’t pander to it | Editorial
records.summary: Confidence in the system is being corroded by cynical campaigns and far-right propaganda – that is the challenge to be confronted There are many areas of policy where public opinion diverges from evidence. Voters overestimate rates of crime, for example. Many will be sceptical of politicians who say today’s streets are safer than they used to be, although that is the reality. The challenge is to find methods of persuasion that don’t belittle the experiences of people who are afraid, and don’t like to be told their fears are unfounded. But there is a different challenge that arises when the cause of public concern is a problem that doesn’t really exist. Many people are angry about “ two-tier policing ” in Britain, supposedly characterised by disproportionately severe enforcement against white people and leniency towards minorities. There is no evidence to support a systemic bias of that kind. By contrast, the data suggests an imbalance of fair treatment goes the other way. People of colour are underrepresented in the police, disproportionately targeted with stop-and-search policies and, if arrested, likelier to have force used against them. records.summary: Emeritus professor Simon Price , Smart Growth UK’s Jon Reeds and former Labour council leader Steve Siddon respond to a column by John Harris John Harris points out the utter inadequacy of Labour’s housing plans, despite Andy Burnham’s passionate advocacy for new social housing ( Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream?, 15 November ). And everyone agrees that we need many more houses. So what’s holding us back? The problem lies in the fiscal rules. At first sight this is puzzling, as borrowing to invest is explicitly allowed (as opposed to borrowing to cover current expenditure). The explanation is the future debt target. Any capital investment increases public debt, and there is a binding debt-to-GDP ratio at the arbitrary and relatively close forecast horizon. Continue reading...

records.title: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter
records.summary: Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James Capon Your report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place ( BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November ). The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. Again, it was for population studies. Continue reading...

Schools should answer to the communities they serve, 13 November ). Jenkins dismisses the work of HMIs as merely a “sniff” of the air and a stroll back to Whitehall, showing a lack of knowledge about their role. HMIs are former school leaders, with a deep knowledge and dedication to educating children and young people. They are as far from the typical civil servant (if there is such a thing) that it is possible to get, and in any case are not based in Whitehall. Jenkins does at least suggest an alternative approach, unlike some who are calling for the abolition of Ofsted, but I really question whether he has thought it through. Parents value the provision of inspection, and most educators agree that assessments are fair – independent YouGov polling showed that 74% of educators believed their most recent inspection was accurate. records.title: Kelly Gough is simply astounding as Desire Under the Elms reaches the heights of Greek tragedy
records.summary: Almeida theatre, London Part-Phaedra and part-Medea, Gough is mesmerising in Ebenezer Bamgboye’s stylised staging of Eugene O’Neill’s family drama You would not know that Eugene O’Neill’s play was originally set on a mid 19th-century farm. This version by director Ebenezer Bamgboye brings modernity with its sleek storytelling, but also nods to the ancient Greek drama O’Neill was emulating in his 1924 play about illicit desire and the father-son fight for land. It makes for a strange mix at first, beguiling and bewildering in equal measure. Bamgboye employs some of the striking theatricality that he brought to his magnetic adaptation of The Lonely Londoners two years ago. It is an original refashioning, the script sharper with less of the exposition that might date it, but the directorial flourishes come so thick and fast that it is stylised to the bone. Bamgboye has previously worked with Rebecca Frecknall (who staged the leaden O’Neill drama A Moon for the Misbegotten last year) and the first half seems to pay too big a debt to her style of work. But this urge started 40 years ago, with what was at first presented as a useful feature I blame the shuffle button. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. records.title: Sublime and ridiculous, but I love the wild experiments of Huddersfield’s contemporary music festival
records.summary: The 49th edition of the new music festival begins this weekend. Where else can you indulge in a world of pure imagination, see the future – and chat over a curry with some of contemporary music’s biggest names? The Huddersfield contemporary music festival – or hcmf , with contemporary-cool lower-case, as it’s styled – celebrates its 49th edition this month, turning the darkness of late November into a beacon of blazing new-music ambition in West Yorkshire. It’s a festival with an extraordinary history. Nowhere else in the UK could you have bumped into Karlheinz Stockhausen and his entourage in a pub in the late 1980s; nowhere else could you have sat in the audience alongside Björk at the town hall; in no other town might you have stumbled on Pierre Boulez, John Cage, Olivier Messiaen and Yvonne Loriod chatting about the best place to have a curry that night. records.title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
records.summary: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. The Game Boy itself used a slow, old Sharp LR35902 processor and a sickly green monochrome screen, but it also came with Tetris and worked for ages on four AA batteries. With sales of 65m, it was vastly more successful than hi-tech rivals such as the Atari Lynx and Sega Game Gear.

records.title: Household rush to stockpile emergency supplies sends British retail sales soaring
records.summary: Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency. records.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
records.summary: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

records.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July

The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. methodology.reliability: A official primary source/catalogue; B established newsroom or independent research; C specialist, advocacy or aggregator; D alternative commentary; E unverified social/community; U unclassified. Grade describes source class, not the truth of a specific claim.
methodology.confidence: Claim confidence is left unassessed unless an upstream collector supplies a numeric value. Source grade is not claim confidence.
methodology.corroboration: The six views reuse the existing archive. Similar stories, repeated posts, syndicated copy or multiple outlets quoting one origin are not independent corroboration. A human must inspect provenance.
methodology.geolocation: Location is shown only when supplied by the source or upstream archive. No location is inferred from a headline.
methodology.limits: This is open-source situational awareness, not intelligence agency coverage, an emergency warning service, a live market terminal or a verified threat assessment.
